utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today, on this Wednesday, I greet the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us. Today, we'll proceed with the examination-in-chief of the witness. I believe that the Prosecution has 35 minutes left to complete its examination-in-chief. Let me also greet the witness who is appearing before us. Let me give the floor to the Prosecutor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, as far as I remember, I have 37 minutes left, but this is not that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, before I start questioning, I would like to ask you kindly to be focused as possible. As you know, we have only 37 minutes left, and I have to go with you some important issues still.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: We spoke yesterday about the disappearance of four young Croats and you described us how you experienced this. Could you please tell me to whom these young Croats who were working in a working brigade were subordinated?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were subordinated to the local command which was a civilian service working in logistics in the locality of Vocin itself, and it provided for the kitchens, the first aid, the police, things like that. So it was work in a warehouse, actually, with supplies, and these civilian authorities had these four young men working for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember where these four young Croats ended up?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said yesterday -- or rather, I said how I encountered the problem when my departure from Vocin to Banja Luka and Serbia, on the 8th. In the evening, 8th of December, 1991, when the evening was being organised, I came across a group of women who were crying, and they told me when I asked them why they were crying that their children weren't at home. Then they went on to tell me that it was a case of four young men who worked in the warehouse, that they didn't come back home on time as they usually did. It was still dark. So I took them to the headquarters to see the commander of the army of the Territorial Defence, Mr. Bojicic, and I asked him in front of them to see what he could do to find out where those young men were, or children, because they were 17 or 18 years old, these young men, young boys. I left Vocin myself, and I didn't know what happened afterwards. Subsequently, I learnt from people who left the area later on that these people were found killed and buried at the entrance to Vocin, if you look at the Slatine-Vocin road. So right before you come to Vocin itself, they were there in an open space.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know who killed them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the information that I received from the population there, or rather from people who worked in the warehouse itself, a man called Todorovic, quite by chance by talking to these people, I learnt that at the time they were deployed in a rather unusual way; that is to say, they were told to go to the village of Balinci to transport ammunition. That was my information told me. That wasn't their task or assignment. They weren't trained to do anything like that, nor should they have been anywhere near the army, let alone to be placed at the disposal of military units in the village of Balinci, which is where there were some volunteers. According to the information that I received and according to what I now know, when these young men were going back, some of those volunteers killed them and buried them on the spot there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Which volunteers? Can you be a bit more specific?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party who were engaged in Vocin at that time. I can't say which group it was, nor can I name the commander, because I received all this information later on from the inhabitants of the village of Vocin who had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that you worked -- you said to Rajko Bojicic that you would hold him responsible and report if the young Croats could not be found. Did you report this, and to whom?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours. The next day I reported it to the command of the Banja Luka Corps, the headquarters there, and Colonel Rankovic, who was the assistant commander at that time for political affairs. He sent me - and this is something I did later on once I received information - anyway, he sent me to Major Djordjevic, who was the military prosecutor at the time in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did this report have any consequences to Rajko Bojicic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know, because the following year, that is to say, 1992, I met Rajko Bojicic in the Pakrac area, and he was a member of the Territorial Defence within the composition of the Yugoslav People's Army there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm interrupting you because you've said something that I find quite significant in relation to the death of these four young men. You said that you met Djordjevic, the military prosecutor, in Banja Luka, and you told him about these events. What did the prosecutor, the military prosecutor, tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the military prosecutor, in an informal talk - because I was told to go look for him when he wasn't in his office - and when I did manage to find him since I was an officer myself, he told me that he must have the necessary data, as far as that was concerned, and that I was to hand over the report officially. I'm talking about 1992 now, so it was two months after the event, the event that took place. I looked for Major Djordjevic so that I could officially make this request; however, I didn't find him there personally. He wasn't working at the job when I arrived ten days later. So, officially, I didn't sign a report, but I did inform the official organs, the prosecutor, and the assistant commander for political affairs in the Banja Luka Corps of the event that had taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But since you were a reserve officer, you know full well that the military prosecutor is competent for crimes committed by military personnel against civilians; therefore, the military prosecutor could have been competent. You went to see him; he was not there. But he must have had an assistant, or was he the only military prosecutor in Banja Luka? Wasn't there anyone else, a colleague of his there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from the 22nd of December till sometime towards the end of February 1992, I worked with the assistant commander of the Banja Luka Corps, General Vukovic, who was the security officer. He was the late Colonel Stevilovic. Now, he was the responsible individual, the individual responsible for all matters of security in the area of the corps when it came to military personnel. Now, since Mr. Stevilovic, together with me, pursuant to an order from Colonel Vukovic, well, I was told to organise some civilian organs. I was in contact with Colonel Stevilovic very frequently, and I told him about the situation, the event. I said that I had to take Major Djordjevic a report, to table a report, because he called me and he said, "All right, we'll see to that." Now, when I attempted to do this on several occasions, I didn't manage to. Perhaps I wasn't responsible enough and I didn't insist enough, but I was dislocated. I was away from Banja Luka, some 60 to 70 kilometres away. I was in Okucani in actual fact, and Banja Luka was in quite a different area. So if you look at the time distance and the actual distance in space, that prevented me from carrying out my moral and civic duty. But I did inform the competent organs, and I was a little surprised to see that there was no formal official request made for an investigation to be undertaken. And when we're referring to Captain Bojicic, he continued within the corps to perform his duties. He wasn't close to me, but I did meet him now and again. I wasn't a policeman for me to be able to investigate anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You went to see Colonel Stevilovic. You told him that you had gone to see the military prosecutor. Then he must have thought that the military prosecutor was competent and he was not supposed to conduct an investigation. He was to wait for the decision by the military prosecutor. Under normal circumstances, the military prosecutor should have reported the matter to the investigative magistrate. Therefore, the colonel you went to see could have thought that he was not to do anything since you had notified the military prosecutor. But if you, yourself, stopped doing anything, then obviously nothing could move in any way. Did you think about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the events that came to pass after the disappearance of those four young men were even more terrible and worse in every respect. First of all, there were crimes; then there was the exodus of the people. Those few of us who had been mobilised again and went to work in the area, were sent to work in the area, faced with a situation of this kind with a humanitarian catastrophe, I didn't have time to think about it. Although, later on, after all these events had passed, I tried to see what had been done, whether anything had been undertaken; and if so, what. But I did not receive an answer. But I have to tell you that the political and security situation in the field was such that it wasn't opportune to discuss it -- the matter either. That wasn't a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When you left Banja Luka, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said, yesterday, that after the exodus of my people from the area of that part of Western Slavonia, I was mobilised again and then deployed to the Banja Luka Corps, so that on the 22nd of December I was to take over the responsibilities and post in the command post of Okucani, which I did. So I left on the 22nd of December and went to Okucani.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I wanted to know, when you were in Banja Luka, you complained or reported to the prosecutor; and, yesterday, you told us it was your intention to go to Belgrade afterwards. Did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did go, Your Honour. On the 9th, that is to say, the next day, I went to my family in Belgrade; and while I was there, that's when the exodus took place, when all the people and the army withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you on that occasion also go to the SRS headquarters; and if so, whom did you meet there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never went to the SRS headquarters. I went to the bureau of the SAO Western Slavonia, and I spoke about that yesterday, Your Honours. And, at the bureau, I was told that the entire people and the soldiers had withdrawn from the area of the municipality of Podravska Slatina; and, previously, I was present when they left Grubisno Polje and Daruvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Sorry. Did you go to the SRS war staff, not to the headquarters, to the SRS war staff?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to the SRS war staff. I happened to go there just by chance in 1992, but already as an officer, as a member of the Okucani local command, because a colleague of mine was going there. He was a captain, an active-duty officer, who was going there for his own personal business -- on his own personal business. So I just went there by chance, not with any intention or purpose or task. I just had the opportunity of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, please do not allow the Prosecutor to interrupt the witness while he's answering the question his was asked. If the Prosecutor doesn't like the answer, that's no reason for him to interrupt the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness was interrupted. Mr. Mussemeyer, was the answer not quite in line with your question or did you want to move to another topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: No. I wanted to remain on this topic. It seems that the witness does not remember or does not understand the question I am putting to him. I wanted to ask him if he ever met Ljubisa Petkovic, the head of the war staff of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's going to answer now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's the only individual whom I met officially. I remember the name of that individual because of the document that Mr. Novacic had with him in the team, the first group of volunteers to Western Slavonia, or more specifically to the village of Ceralije, which is where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Where did you meet him, and what was the reason for this?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat, Your Honours. I said a moment ago, and that was how it was. Anyway, it was the end of January or beginning of February 1992, when, together with an officer from my command, Mr. Zarko, I went to Belgrade, I went to visit my family and he was going efficiently to the general staff. Then, together with him, I went to see Mr. Petkovic. I wouldn't know that it was Petkovic had he not introduced himself. Then I asked him, "Are you the same person who sent that first group of volunteers?" He said, "Yes." Then I made some observations with respect to aid and assistance and behaviour and conduct, and he had his own position on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What did you tell him? Did you complain or did you praise the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I said how things were, how things stood. I said that the volunteers that they had sent, that first group, certainly acted as I read out in the instructions. But as to the other groups, I can't say in general, but many of the members of the volunteers, many of the volunteers, behaved irresponsibly. They weren't under the command and control of the Territorial Defence, and there were grounds to suspect that they had carried out a series of crimes in the area in which they were active.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you have any information if criminals have been among these volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I did not have an opportunity to talk to the volunteers, and that wasn't my job either so I didn't interview them. But from the information that I received from my colleagues and friends who did have contact with them, specifically some policemen who had worked in Vocin, there were volunteers who, because they voluntarily went up to report to the unit, they no longer had to serve their prison sentence in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I would like to show the witness 65 ter number 782. This is a document which has already been admitted as P225, but it fits into the context now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Before the document shows up on the monitor, Mr. Witness, please, what was Mr. Petkovic's reaction?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Petkovic did not accept my descriptions and complaints. What I told him was that these people didn't help us out. They did a disservice to us because the local population were afraid of them. And according to certain witnesses, they had perpetrated certain acts and crimes in Vocin, and those crimes will ultimately be ascribed to the people there. So I was speaking from the aspects of protecting my people over there, my nation. Mr. Petkovic questioned and challenged the fact that anything like that could have been perpetrated by his volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he already has taken some measures to prevent that -- the acting against the law?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a highly leading question. If the answer was that Ljubisa Petkovic denied the fact that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party perpetrated crimes, then this next question is impossible: Did he tell you that he took certain steps to provide the violation of the law?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mussemeyer. If the witness complains about the behaviour of the volunteers, and if Mr. Petkovic tells him that he has no information about this, it's quite difficult to imagine that the witness asked him if he had taken any measures.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: To prevent the violation of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It was not the witness who asked for this; it was the answer of Mr. Petkovic, as far as I know. But before we discuss about it, I would like to have the witness to look at the document which is now shown on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: This is an authorisation signed by Ljubisa Petkovic, the 10th of December, 1991, and it says in the first sentence: "For the purpose of establishing law and order and control in Western Slavonia, Milan Dobrilovic ... is entitled, is authorised, to supervise all volunteers." This document wouldn't make any sense. So, Mr. Witness, could you please comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information about the relationship between the volunteers and the Territorial Defence, and cooperation among them, I'm certain that my Territorial Defence staff harmonised with the staff that sent those people to Western Slavonia in the first place. However, when we look at this document and when I look at the date - it was in Belgrade on the 10th of December - what I can say is that that was too late, because on the 13th of December all the people moved out. Of course, there was the other part of Western Slavonia towards Okucani, Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when you went to the war staff - and we have the address of the war staff here in this document; it's Obridska Street 1; we even have the phone number, 011/456-745 - is that where you met Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour, in that office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you entered the building, was there a flag there, were there guards, or was it a civilian-looking building or a military-type building? In your recollection, what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I remember, Your Honour, is that it was a civilian building. I'm sure there was some writing there, but it was such a long time ago and there was no need for me to pay attention to things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you saw Dobrilovic, was he wearing civilian clothes or a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where did you see him? Did you see him on a corridor, on a staircase, in a lift? Where did you actually see him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In his office, Your Honour, that's where I saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So were there any maps in his office, were there any computers, any maps with any arrows like in any standard war staff? Was it just an ordinary office as you can see in civilian life, or was it an office of a military nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't -- it was a civilian office, but with all the characteristic features of the party belonging to the state. Perhaps there were some posters and pictures. I can't remember what they were, but I'm certain that there were the emblems of the Serbian Radical Party and things like that. But I was interested more in Mr. Petkovic because he was somebody I had already met. I mean I met him -- his name in the documents, I came across his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if Mr. Petkovic was in a position of a military nature, according to this document, we can see that there is a war staff. So one can reasonably expect to see maps and a whole series of telephones where he would be in contact permanently with the volunteers on the ground. If he is a chief of staff, there would be a lot of movement in the office, a lot of information coming in at all times; or if we imagine a different scenario, a standard civilian office which is not military in any way. This is what I'm interested in, and I'm waiting for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sure there were maps there; but what kind of maps and anything else, it's difficult for me to remember because I was in many other offices later on. But I'm sure that there was a lot of coming and going. People were rushing through, but I didn't know the people so I didn't pay much attention to any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question: You are the first witness who has been there. So my question can be put to other witnesses, but it so happens that you were there. Now, when you walk into this building, did you have the feeling you were walking into a military building or a civilian building which was the headquarters of a political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was certainly a civilian building, and I'm sure I would have recognised it if it were a military building. Now, after visiting the headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party, I later went to the military building, or a military building. So that was quite different and the behaviour of the people in that building was quite different. So I have to assert that this was, indeed, a civilian building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you went to see Mr. Petkovic to complain about the behaviour of the volunteers, given Mr. Petkovic's answer, why didn't you then ask to see Mr. Seselj in person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had no official function, no official duty. I would have had to ask for my superior, the late General Vukovic, to do this. But I did not consider that the president of a political party should participate in discussions of military issues. I didn't think so then and I don't think so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you already told us that the exodus which started the 13th of December, 1991, as you said. What was the reason for this exodus?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reason was primarily the civil war that happened there and then the isolation of the area, the disorganisation of the government, the civilian structures. All this time the media, both on the Serbian and also on the Croatian side, constantly frightened people by saying what might happen to those people, and there was constant pressure being exerted. I have to admit that the soldiers who were there, the Territorial Defence, the formal and informal groups that were there, were constantly frightening people. If a house burnt down in a street and everybody knew that the house had been torched, I'm sure everybody would be afraid. I'm now speaking of the general psychological situation, and especially when some people had already been evacuated. I have to say that some of the youngest and oldest inhabitants had already been evacuated from the area. On the 8th of December, two municipalities were already vacated. All the people had moved out. The municipalities of Grubisno Polje and Daruvar. The people in the Podravska Slatina municipality were there still, but on a temporary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if crimes had been committed during this exodus; and if so, against whom?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. From my conversations with those people, when I came across the people who were fleeing or who had fled - as I said on the 9th I left Vocin early in the morning - and up until the 15th of December, I didn't know that the people had left because I was in Serbia. But when I heard about this, in Banja Luka I went and met quite a few of those people when I was mobilised again, and I learnt from them that several civilians had been killed there, or several dozen civilians, that is. Then, later on, I received information that the number was about 40 civilians, most of them elderly. If I were to explain this in detail, it happened on a location near the road along which the people and the soldiers were withdrawing. In that street, 42 or 43 people were killed, both men and women.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of these victims?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most often, people say they were all Croats, but I think there were also Hungarians and others among them; but, conditionally speaking, they were non-Serbs. They were Croats, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you have any information who committed these crimes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know except for two names. I don't know the names of the others, but I happen to know that some persons were from my neighbourhood whom I knew, whom I had spoken to. There were four women. They saw a group that did that -- the group that did that. And in that group consisting of six or seven persons who wore masks, they recognised two persons from Vocin, two young men from Vocin, by their voices, and they told me their names. They were convinced that the others were members of the volunteer units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I know that it takes a lot of time to have the map on the monitor. Could you please already put again the map 65 ter number 2868 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I will come back to the reason of the exodus. So it was not that -- sorry, it would be leading. It was not that the Croats forced the Serbs out of this region?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This kind of question cannot be put. You can't say it was not that the Croats forced the Serbs out of this region. This is unprecedented during examination-in-chief in adversarial proceedings. This is really impermissible, what the Prosecutor is doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be better to ask the witness why there was such an exodus and who left, and then you can put your other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have the Serbs of this region been forced to leave the region or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you have any information who forced them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the attitude of my country, of their country towards them, those were the conditions that were created and they took those weapons. Then propaganda, there was a lot of propaganda and it frightened people. People were afraid they would be killed. They were afraid they would suffer the same fate that their parents had suffered 40 or 50 years before, and so they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you have any information --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another objection. I think the witness should clarify what he means by "their country." I think he should state precisely what country he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a question you could put during cross-examination. You're referring to the state. Which state do you mean, the former Yugoslavia? Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the former Yugoslavia had six states within it. Each of the republics was a state under the constitution of 1974. So the Republic of Croatia was also a state. I was referring to the Republic of Croatia, to its official government at the time. We would need more time to explain what they did. There's not enough time here to explain all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that the Serbs who had left and had left forcibly, if I understand you correctly, had to leave because the Croats - we are talking about the Republic of Croatia - did nothing about it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it did everything to get them to leave. That's the conclusion I might draw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you are saying that they did everything they could to make sure they left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite so, Your Honour. That was the atmosphere that prevailed there at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, you told us that people told you that two locals were among the persons who committed these crimes and the other ones were allegedly volunteers. What was the role of the locals?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The locals had the role of showing which houses were Croatian houses and who were the Serbs, who were the Croats, because otherwise you couldn't tell them apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know who of them committed the crimes? Were the locals involved in the commitment of the crimes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I have, which I believe - I heard this from eye-witnesses and also I attended various trials where this was proved also against me - two local people from Vocin and a group of volunteers participated in this, Serbian volunteers. It was a group consisting of six or seven persons, and it's possible there was another group also because this was a large area. But according to the information I had, the persons who told me this had protected a group of Croats, people called Doric from the end of the village. They protected them, and they said there were no more Croatian houses there. So, evidently, this was an attack on the other nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting. You are giving us some information. You said that there were proceedings before a court, so I conclude, therefore, that these 40 to 42 people that had been killed, both men and women, these people had been killed by volunteers and two locals from Vocin. It seems that there was a trial as a result of this. So these two locals from Vocin, were they prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. An indictment was raised against them. I don't know whether they were convicted, but a trial was held; and from these events - and I was accused of having committed those in 1995 in Bjelovar - there was a trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there was a trial in 1995. Where do you say that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the district court, now it's the county court, in Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And were you being charged during this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was charged for being responsible for those crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What happened after that? Were you acquitted? What was the verdict of the tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The verdict was -- well, there was a law on abolition under which I was acquitted. The court established that, in view of my formal duties and obligations, I could not be held responsible, especially as I wasn't in Vocin at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, what about the other people? Were they convicted? Those people who committed the crimes, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the group that was tried when I was tried, there were five of us. One among them, a Bosnian, was convicted of crimes committed a little before that and in connection with that crime, but the crime was not proved against him in court. However, I had the opportunity of seeing the indictment - and now it's available to the public - and I think that the names on that indictment include the names of those two men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said this is a public indictment; it can be read by anybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, and Serbia. This is not a document that the Judges of this Tribunal can see, I don't know why, but I would like this to be recorded on the transcript. It's through my questions that I discovered that there was a trial on facts which the Prosecutor is questioning you about. Now, were there any lawyers? Did you have a lawyer at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. There were counsel. First I had an ex officio counsel, and then the United Nations recruited a lawyer to defend me because I was working for the UN at the time of my arrest as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the United Nations paid for a lawyer. The volunteers of the SRS who were convicted at the same time you were, if I understood you correctly, you were five -- there were five of you, and there were five people and all the other people were volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. All those five accused, along with me, were from Podravska Slatina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the volunteers who were there, they escaped from any prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether there are any proceedings ongoing in Croatia against the volunteers. I never had any opportunity of seeing something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I feel one cannot so lightly overlook the fact that the OTP has not disclosed to me the information on the trial against Mr. Kulic in Croatia when crimes in Vocin were ascribed to him. The OTP knew that there had been proceedings against Mr. Kulic in Croatia, and this is mentioned in one sentence of the statement signed by this witness. So it was their duty to obtain the entire record from the court in Bjelovar and to disclose it to me and to Your Honours when the trial began. I think it's very important to use those documents in examining this witness, especially from the point of view where we see that the Croatian authorities never indicted a single volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party for any crime committed in Croatia. I think this is very important, this material, and I think you should sanction the OTP for not having done its work properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, it seems very surprising to discover that a witness who is coming here to testify - he is a Prosecution witness - when this witness was mentioned in an indictment pertaining to crimes that were committed in Vocin. Fortunately, the witness was acquitted, but we see that there were no volunteers at all mentioned in this indictment. Perhaps the Prosecutor felt that he had nothing to do with these crimes, which is an important piece of information. This could, in fact, benefit the accused or mention of these volunteers in the indictment, that these volunteers had disappeared and that is why they were not prosecuted. Nonetheless, this document, i.e., this indictment, should have been disclosed to the accused, who quite clearly has not received it. This is something which we discover through the questions and answers. Now, is the Prosecution able to tell us today whether, A, it has had this document? If it hasn't, why the Prosecution wasn't concerned about getting a copy? Then, C, why not tell the accused about all of this? Some of this might be exculpatory or not. I am unable to assess this because none of us have actually seen this document. So can you tell us anything about this; or tell us that, like what we are able to see today, we are just discovering that there was such a trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I am not in a position to tell you if the OTP is in the possession of this document. I will find that out and let the Trial Chamber know about it. That the witness has been accused is not a secret. It appears in the statement, as far as I remember, of the witness. And as the witness has been acquitted and he wasn't there at the time the crimes were committed, he was not in Vocin, it may be - this is what I think - that the Prosecution never asked for this document. But exact information I will give you when I have the chance to check this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this witness stated himself that he was acquitted outside the legal proceedings. He said by abolition. As far as I can recall, there was an amnesty in 1975 [as interpreted] in Croatia. It may have been an abolition. I'm not sure whether it was abolition or amnesty; but, in any case, it is an out-of-court form of acquittal. It's done by the executive branch of government. I don't know whether it's the president of the state or someone else. Usually, it's the chief of the executive branch of government who proclaims an abolition and the parliament that proclaims an amnesty. But neither the one nor the either is within the competence of the judicial branch of government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you have said does have legal consequences when you said you'd been acquitted because the tribunal drew its own legal conclusions. Now, in light of what you've said, I understood that a law had been adopted in parliament, a law that amnestied those events that were tied to what had happened. And as you were prosecuted in relation to these events, the tribunal then applied the law and stated that there was no case to answer given the adoption of the new law. That is why you were not convicted and you were not found guilty, either guilty or innocent. You are a very educated man. You know a lot of things. Is this the reason? Is it because this new law was adopted that you were neither convicted nor formally acquitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I expressed my reservations in advance. I'm not very familiar with the terminology and the legal proceedings. I may have expressed myself erroneously. In Croatia, there is a special term that they use for the law on amnesty. They call it the law on forgiveness. That's the literal term and that's what I should have said instead of using foreign words. But under pressure, the government of the Republic of Croatia and the parliament enacted a law whereby all members of armed units, who did not commit any crimes, were relieved - I'm speaking this now and I'm saying this in my own words - and they were exempt from any further prosecution. And based on that law, I was released because they could not find anything else in the legal proceedings that they could hold me responsible for. They couldn't hold me responsible for the events in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, now the witness has explained it's probably not abolition, because abolition is an expression of presidential mercy. It's an individual act for a suspect, an accused, or a convict. But if it's a law, the Prosecutor should have disclosed to us that law because this amnesty applies to certain crimes and not to other crimes. So we have to see that law of 1995 in Croatia to see precisely what crimes, because I'm using the word "crime" now in the broad sense, even armed rebellion. We have to see which ones the amnesty applies to and which ones it doesn't. We need that law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently, there was a law on amnesty and the witness took advantage of that. It would probably be useful to get to know this document, but you probably do not have it, or do not have it here now. Everybody is aware of this problem. Please proceed, Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, how much time do I have? Can you tell me, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Mussemeyer, you have 13 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, you see on the monitor the map you have already commented on at the beginning of your examination-in-chief. Could you please show us the way where the exodus took place and where the crimes against the 40 Croats you mentioned happened, on this map.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Vocin itself, in the street, or rather, on the road which goes from the direction of Vocinski Hum, where you see it's been circled to the north of Vocin, so in that direction; and then it goes to the centre of Vocin. In that street on that road, which is approximately 700 metres to one kilometre long, I don't recall right now the number of households or family houses, but I know for certain that at the entrance to Vocin, on this road I'm indicating, there's a house belonging to a family. I think their last name is Stimac. They live near some acquaintances of mine, and 15 persons were killed in or near that house. But in the proceedings I mentioned, in the trial against me and in some other trials where I was a witness, a lot was said about that, and I knew that there were documents to show that this had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding these 40 people who were killed, can you tell me whether there were, for most of them, killed in the street? Because you said 15 of them were found in a house. Were they killed in the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those 15 were killed inside that house. All the others were killed in yards or in front of yards or on the road, either near their houses or in their own courtyards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To your knowledge, were they killed because they had been detained and then executed, or did some people arrive there and start shooting at everyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were killed because they were Croats and because, in my opinion, when people were leaving, they were angry, frustrated, and a group was out of control and did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I've understood you correctly, these crimes were committed at the very moment when the Serb population was withdrawing from Vocin. Everybody was leaving. It was probably chaos there. Then at this particular point, some individuals, the two from Vocin plus, according to you, some volunteers, then these people killed the Croats who lived in these houses. Is that the way things happened according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was total chaos. From everything that I heard and saw in that chaos and in the withdrawal and along that road, the people that happened to be there who didn't take shelter and were members of the -- and were ethnic Croats, quite simply that group was out of control and committed the crime.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness is now testifying about things that took place 400 kilometres away from him. I'd just like to draw your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. It did not escape me because you, Witness, were not there. What you're telling us is based on what other people told you. You may have been able to read about it in the press. You're telling us maybe what you heard during the trial because you attended the trial and these events were probably mentioned during the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I still live there today and I know all those people, all the people who were there on that day, not directly present in the courtyard, but who met that group of individuals and recognised them. So they're people who are alive today. I'm in contact with them, I know them because I lived there, and I'm close to them for that simple reason. I was interested to know whether they knew who committed it, and they said, yes, but they couldn't say what their names were. They were all wearing masks, but they said that they recognised a young man at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we come to the basic question of why the Prosecution hasn't called in as witnesses some of the people who had recognised the perpetrators of the crime, not somebody who heard from others what they might have seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. You say that they were wearing masks and that some of them were recognised because of their voice. What about the others? How were they identified? How is it possible to say that they were volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to speculate and guess. What I heard from these people was this: They heard -- well, they were in fear because they heard shooting and saw dead bodies, and then they came across a group of people; and amongst those people amongst that group, well, they were afraid of people in the group because they were on the road moving in all that chaos. They had organised themselves for a journey, and they were running across the road to put in there things to join the column to flee from there. So they weren't looking for this group. It's that this group of people was looking to them to ask whether there were other Croatian houses there, because -- and from the testimony of the people that I'm referring to, I am recounting what happened and I am convinced of that myself. Now, you can ask yourselves why I wasn't there, but I lived with those people before and I still live with those people today. I know the people and their mentality very well, and I know what I can be sure of. That's why I'm testifying in this way and saying what I'm saying without violating anybody's rights or placing anybody in an unfavourable or unpleasant situation, because I've had occasion to go through situations like that myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I've understood you correctly, the two individuals from Vocin who executed these people, they still live in Vocin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. No, far from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They left, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you already -- you told us where the crimes happened in Vocin. Can you tell us where the exodus initially started? It was not in Vocin, as far as I am informed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, again, Mr. President. Again, a leading question, and I consider this to be impertinent on the part of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is, indeed, a very leading question. Can you please rephrase it to obtain the same result eventually?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he's already gained the result with his leading question. Now the witness has a chance to adapt himself to the question, and it doesn't matter what version of the question he comes up with now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The answer may be different if the question is rephrased. You never know. Mr. Mussemeyer, can you please start from the very beginning without asking any type of leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, for me this question is not leading. I asked if there existed another village where the exodus took place, and I did not mention the name of this place. I only said that, obviously, it didn't start in Vocin in. For me, this is not leading. The aim of my question is another village, and I did not take or put the name of this village into the mouth of the witness. I want to hear it from him. So with all due respect, this is not leading from me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mr. Mussemeyer, you are telling us that according to your information, and so on and so forth. The problem is that we need to know whether this particular witness told you that the exodus did not start in Vocin. If it's not this particular witness who told you that, you can't say, "I was informed," and put your question that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It was exactly this witness who told me that it started in another village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please answer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then you're right. Then you're right. Your question was not leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not recall the witness saying that here in court, in the courtroom, that the exodus started in another place, and you can put me right if you have evidence that he did. Perhaps the witness told him that during the proofing session outside the courtroom, which means that he doesn't have the right to use it in court in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I surmise that he told you about it during the proofing session and you're now bringing that up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly the reason I am asking this, and I did on purpose not mention the name of another village. I want to hear it from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fine. But you could have dealt with it the following way and you could have said: "There was an exodus in Vocin. To your knowledge, this particular or specific exodus, did it take place somewhere else in the region?" Then he could have said that, no, it was not specific to Vocin; it started in another village. But your purpose was to find out in this chaos whether the exodus was also happening in other villages. Witness, now you understand the question. What is your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, during my testimony, I mentioned, once or twice I think, that before the event of the 13th of December, the people from the area of Grubisno Polje municipality, specifically on the 30th of October or rather the 1st of November, passed across Vocin in its exodus towards Bosnia. Now, on the 7th, 8th, and 9th of December, this was done from the villages in the Daruvar municipality. About the 13th, or rather the 12th, I happened to learn this by chance from the inhabitants of Lisicine village, which is north of Vocin on this map. You can see it, Lisicine, it is about # kilometres away. Colonel Jovan Trbojevic was born there, and that's his native village. They started out on the evening before the 13th, which means the 12th in the evening. I heard that from my friends in that village, and I didn't know that for a long time. I learned this perhaps a year ago. So this whole wave of exodus started in Lisicine, and the entire process was prepared because two municipalities under that pressure had already left in the previous month. If that suffices as an explanation, that's what I would like to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that there was in flow of people, this wave of people. We can very well picture the situation, especially in Vocin, and we can very well imagine what was the state of mind of somebody living in Vocin. But did the authority, the military authority, the TO or the civilian authority, take any type of measure in order to preserve public law and order? Were measures taken or was it the general debacle? Was everybody running for it, and was there a total lack of authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think the latter would be closest to the truth. Nobody had any control over anything. There was a total lack of authority. I'm saying that for the simple reason that this region, 25 settlements, including parts of Orahovica and Podravska Slatina municipalities, they did not have a structure of civilian authority. They didn't come across that kind of structure. They had to establish their own power and authority. They tried to do so but were unsuccessful. So the only institutions and authority that existed were in the form of military institutions and the Territorial Defence and Territorial Defence staffs; although, I have to admit that at the end of October already the assembly was set up and civilian structures were to follow, but this was just an early attempt. So when the exodus took place, it was an ongoing process, it didn't take place only on the 13th; but on the 13th, it comprised 25 villages and hamlets. But, in fact, it took place over a month and a half, from the 30th of October right up to the 13th of December, because if I mentioned municipality of Grubisno Polje, which is at a distance of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. But what was the JNA doing at the time? Why weren't they on the spot, or were they running away as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The units and services of the Yugoslav People's Army were not on the spot, not in the area of Podravska Slatina and Grubisno Polje and Daruvar, and their active components were not there. They were somewhere at the line of Pakrac-Bucje; that is to say, the JNA units were at a distance of about 30 kilometres away. However, the Yugoslav People's Army, or rather the Banja Luka Corps, covered logistics, organisation, assistance in various forms. I wasn't in the staff, so I can't speak specifically about that, in the staff of Western Slavonia. But based on the information that I had, Colonel Trbojevic arrived as the commander, as a trained and educated commander, and was probably very well capable of conducting that -- those affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The JNA was 30 kilometres away from there, but there were roads in the region. It would have taken them 30 minutes to arrive. In the JNA you had a military police as well, and it is the duty of the military police to preserve law and order and control traffic on the roads. From what you say, I understand that there was none of this happening and that the JNA was actually relying on the TO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. The JNA, well, in talking to members of the Yugoslav People's Army in the Banja Luka Corps, that's what they said, that their units, their brigade, from the line of Pakrac and Pozega, that they would not go anywhere else; whereas, the Territorial Defence would help in the organisation. That was my information both from officials in the corps and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, can you tell us where this village of Lisicine is situated on the map?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain this to you, to describe it, but I'll show you on the map with my pen. Here it is, where it says "Lisicine." So I would say it's some five kilometres north of Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And is the road we can see between Vocin and Lisicine the way the exodus took place?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's the line of the exodus, or one of the directions that the exodus took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation why the exodus on that day started in Lisicine?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to information that I received, and I said I was very much surprised from the locals of Lisicine going back to Croatia frequently to their houses that had been restored in Croatia, they told me that on the evening of the 12th, Colonel Trbojevic, passing by or visiting the village, told the people to come to Vocin if they were afraid and spend the night there. By saying that, he influenced the exodus of everyone. It wasn't only individuals from Lisicine that came, it was the whole village that was on the move and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can I please move the map with the annotations of the witness into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, a number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P266.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, another issue. You told us, in the beginning, that you have been forced from -- you had been forced into the TO. Has there been a second event when you had been forced into the TO or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With my departure on the 9th of December from Vocin and the withdrawal of people from Vocin, their exodus, the exodus of that nation, my role ceased. There was no more Territorial Defence, no more staff; and I went to Serbia, found myself in Serbia. I tried to find a job of some kind because my family was there. Anyway, I was arrested, or rather I considered it being that I was arrested; but I was taken into custody, detained on the street, because I had Podravska Slatina licence plates on my car. They asked me whether I was such and such. I gave them my name, surname. They asked to see my ID and they escorted me, and they told me to sign the mobilisation call-up. I think it was on the 16th or 17th; I can't be quite sure. Anyway, I once again -- well, I no longer got into the car. I was escorted to Mitrovica and taken from Bijeljina to Banja Luka; and in Banja Luka, I received my deployment orders in the Banja Luka Corps command. The local commander is a reserve officer in Okucani.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where you have been arrested; and if you know, by whom?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I considered that I had been arrested; although, the men told us that they weren't actually arresting me. But there was a policeman in uniform. It was in the place called Sid. I wanted to work there. There was the meat-processing industry, and they told me that they needed officers there. Anyway, a civilian -- well, we found ourselves in front of the Secretariat for National Defence, which is the institution that mobilises people, and they said that under the circumstances they had every right to mobilise me. Now, I asked them what the alternative was, what choice did I have, and they said that if I refused I would be arrested. Now, later on I saw other people. I met other people. I'd like to take this opportunity to say that many people from my region who were refugees in Serbia were mobilised, so that I wasn't an exception. But, anyway, it hit me hard because not then and not afterwards did I want to be a volunteer. I would have liked to have been a volunteer for something that I chose to be, not something I was forced to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have five minutes, Mr. Mussemeyer, to complete your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, does the word "Daruvar Agreement" say anything to you; and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Daruvar Agreement was the first peace agreement between the Serbs and the Croatian state, and I was one of the participants or signatories of the agreement. It is, if I can put it this way, a forerunner to the Erdut Agreement, or, which should have been more favourable, an agreement that was just drafted, the Z4 Agreement. Yes, I do know what the Daruvar Agreement was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have there been opponents of this agreement amongst the Serbs or amongst the Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A group of people in Western Slavonia to which I belonged considered that we should use some of the advantages and establish, with the help of the international community, a peace -- or set up peace negotiations. This is something that the international community offered us, that we should negotiate with the Croatian state, because we were in an area which was a junction for various international roads. So I was an advocate of that; and with the Daruvar Agreement, I thought we could help people to have a different life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: My question was: Have there been opponents against this agreement; and if so, who were they?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were opponents. They were first of all the government or most of the government of the Republika Srpska Krajina led by Hadzic and Martic, because after that, sometime later, I and the group were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who arrested you and what happened to you later on?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested by the assistant -- by Martic's assistant, Zrkovic, Krsto Zrkovic, or his group in Okucani, and I was detained in Knin; and with the other people in the group, they kept me in detention in Glina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: How long have you been in detention?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about four months, I was in detention for about four months. Then with pressure from the international community, because I was a UN employee and some other people, well, there were not sufficient grounds in the indictment for accusing us. So they let us go, but they still persecuted us. Matters didn't end there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have you been arrested a second time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't arrested a second time. I was arrested again but in 1995 by the Croatian state. However, somebody else was arrested for a second time, and he was my friend Dzakula in Belgrade, when we're talking about persecution by the Krajina authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have you ever been interviewed by Milan Martic about the Daruvar Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was arrested on the 21st of September, 1993, in Knin, Milan Martic personally talked to me. He said, "Well, Kulic, why did you need that? What did you need that for? You were a respected officer," and things along that line. "Why did you betray us Croats," and things like that. So he tried to persuade me that what I was doing was not correct, but I told Martic privately that that was the only solution, that negotiations were the only way out. I didn't see how things could be settled in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if others have been beaten up during their detention? By "others" I mean the other persons who participated in the negotiations of the Daruvar Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, three of us, Your Honour. Three participants in the signing of the Daruvar Agreement were detained, were held in detention. Mr. Dzakula and I were received from -- well, were beaten from Mr. Martic; not from him actually but his men, his people, beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I have no further questions, but I have some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: -- there's one observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj said in this transcript, at line 24:7, there is mentioned the year "1975." I think this is an error or it might a mistake during translation. It should be "1995," if I am right. Could we check this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. This has been recorded now. Now, the best would be to have the break now. We'll have a 20-minute break and resume with Mr. Seselj's cross-examination after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing and we shall start with the cross-examination. Mr. Seselj has two hours for his cross-examination. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kulic, at the beginning of the examination-in-chief, when asked by Judge Antonetti why you changed your mind and did not insist on protective measures, you said that circumstances have changed. What I would like to know is what circumstances induced you earlier on when you testified in the Slobodan Milosevic trial to ask for protective measures and how these circumstances have changed so that you don't need protective measures anymore?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, part of my family lives in the Republic of Serbia and the other part in the Republic of Croatia. As of 2002 until today, both in the Republic of Serbia and in the Republic of Croatia, as regards the security of citizens, communications, and so on, the situation has changed considerably. I think people are much freer. In any case, my direct answer is: The members of my family have agreed for me to testify in open session. This had been my wish before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're aware that The Hague OTP, for a full five years, perhaps more since your first statement, has considered you a witness in this case against me. Have you ever felt that you needed protective measures because you were in danger from me personally, you or your family?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have known for a year, since I was contacted by this Court, that the Court is interested in my testimony in this case. Previously, it had to do with another case. As regards Dr. Seselj, I see no reason or need as regards him personally. I'm not saying that there may not be a threat from members of his party but not from him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the members of the Serbian Radical Party are dangerous, that they might pose a threat to somebody's life or work?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the members of the Radical Party, well, I have relatives and acquaintances who are members of that party and some of them were or still are refugees from Croatia, and I'm sure that they do not approve of my testimony before this Tribunal today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it was the reaction you expected from your relatives who are members of the Serbian Radical Party. There was no other reason. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was just the assumption that led me with respect to the security of my family and myself in the past period. I'm not saying it's not possible today, but I think that the possibility has been much reduced. I just mentioned this as an example when Dr. Seselj asked me that question. In the area I hail from, it's still not completely safe and secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And now you live in Podravska Slatina, as I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I live in the place called Slatina, which used to be called Podravska Slatina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how do you earn your living there now?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as regards my personal CV and biography, I would rather not answer these questions if they are not linked to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you have to answer every question I put, because I'm challenging your credibility as a Prosecution witness. So it is your duty to answer every question. What do you live on?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, would you respond? Do I have to answer questions that are not directly linked to the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are proceedings which may seem different to the ones than you are familiar with in your country. The accused is entitled to put questions to you in order to check the credibility of the witness; and, therefore, he is entitled to ask you what you live off and what you are currently doing. I, by the way, did put the question to you and I asked you just before you took the solemn declaration: Do you have an occupation? You responded by saying that you are retired. I concluded thereafter that you weren't working and that you have a pension perhaps, but I did not look into the matter any further. But Mr. Seselj is entitled to ask you what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am not retired. I just told you I was not employed. My status now is that I am not employed but I have not reported to the job centre because I am working under contract for various NGOs. Right now, I am working on issues of the return of refugees from Croatia, as regards finding accommodation for them, welfare, the return of their houses, and so on. These cases can last, well, a year or six months, and I'm working -- the one I'm working on here is for a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What organisations are you working for?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've worked for the Serbian Democratic Forum --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreter did not catch the name. THE WITNESS: [Interpretation]-- An organisation from Rome. Now on the Pakrac region, I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down and pause between question and answer, and could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go slowly. The interpreters have difficulty keeping up with you. You're speaking, both of you, the same language and the interpreters are finding it hard. So please wait for the person who has asked a question to finish his question before you answer. But if you answer instantly, then we will face a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, how many trials in Croatia did you testify in, trials of Serbs accused of war crimes, up till now?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in one trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who was that trial against?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was against Branko Oliver from Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've already said that when doing your regular military service, you completed the school for reserve officers, that you became -- you acquired rank as second lieutenant, and then you got employment in the All People's Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. I was the first employee in a staff that was being established, and my status was that of an employee in the secretariat of All People's Defence. Later on, I was an operative in that same staff. That was the precise name of the job, "operative."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who was the chief of that staff while you were an operative there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The late Matija Perkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how long did you work in that staff, until when?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: other issues, so I shall give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You told us, according to your own statement, on the 28th of August, 1991, you left Podravska Slatina and came to Vocin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how was it then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 29th, the second day of the Ascension, I arrived in Lukavac village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did you get to Vocin?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second day, i think it was the 30th, but I'm not quite sure. I didn't measure time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who put you up in Vocin?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was accommodated in the house of the late Nikola Radosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Has he got anything to do with Savo Radosevic? Is he a relative?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was Savo Radosevic's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Savo Radosevic was your closest friend, as far as I know; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was he a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A really close friend?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How close?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then, in Vocin, you became involved in the Territorial Defence staff. You said here that you were forcibly taken there; whereas, in fact, you joined the staff on a voluntary basis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were forced to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you have a piece of paper to prove that you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1991, all my private affairs were at least five times taken away by different forces in the region, so I couldn't have kept them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In September 1991, a unit of the Territorial Defence from Vocin killed more than 20 Croatian civilians in the village of Cetekovci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
