utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is right, then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Balinci and Cojluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What happened in Cetekovci?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a central locality which in public and otherwise, especially with the Croatian side, was used as a place and address to which this massacre was sent. Well, there were killings without doubt, but it didn't happen that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And those Balinci and Cojluk, can they be called hamlets close to Cetekovci?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They come in front and afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it's the general Cetekovci area.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many civilians were killed over there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: More than 20?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the press wrote, and in some trials that figure came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that at your trial?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proceedings against me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Some of those Croatian civilians were -- had their throats slit with a knife.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I refused to accept that form. Your Honours, what that was about was that photographs of massacred people in Bjelovar at the trial were brought into me. They were shown to me, I don't know for what reasons. I have the feeling that this was pressure at the time against me; but, in any case, I felt unprotected and abused because I didn't know the people. I was never over there, so it had nothing to do with me at all, except that I was very sorry that anybody had lost their life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the basis of those photographs, it could be seen that not all the people were killed by firearms but some of them were killed by sharp objects.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I refused to look at the photographs and didn't look at them; but that's what I heard, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You refused to look at the photographs?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You took part in that attack itself at Balinci and Cojluk, did you not, the Cetekovci hamlets?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your honours, that's not true. What Mr. Seselj is saying is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, it's true. It's true, and the Croatian authorities know that very well and that's why they raised an indictment against you. They did not accuse you for the crime in Vocin when you weren't in Western Slavonia, but for the crimes dated to September when you were in Vocin; isn't that right? You kept quiet about that a moment ago before this Trial Chamber, when you said why the Croatian authorities persecuted you. You said that they persecuted for things that happened at the time when you weren't in Western Slavonia at all. You said that in this courtroom a moment ago in this courtroom; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that, Judges, you remember Mr. Kulic saying that, that he said that they released him from prison and amnestied him because he wasn't at the scene of the crime at the time. Now we have a fresh piece of information that he was at the scene of this crime and that he took part in this crime, and then we'll see why he was released from prison in due course. We'll come to that. Anyway --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. Apparently, Witness, according to Mr. Seselj - as far as I'm concerned, I don't have a single document about this - but, apparently, you took part in the perpetration of a crime against 20 Croats who, allegedly, were killed with knives. Were you there? Were you not there? What do you have to say about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've already answered that question. I said when I was mobilised and what duties I had; and in that connection, I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to look at the evidence that was presented in the district court of Bjelovar in the proceedings there in 1995. Now, the various constructs that Mr. Seselj is now making are calculated. Well, he's not interested in what I know about the facts of this case. He is insinuating various other things. Now, I reject all that and I have taken the solemn declaration before you here to tell the truth. Everything I have told you is the truth and I can prove it. I consider this to be a personal attack which can jeopardise my security, Your Honours, and that is Mr. Seselj's aim. He has no other objective but to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, had the Prosecution supplied us with the data from the court in Podravska Slatina, you would have been able to see that this is what it said in the indictment against Mr. Kulic, and that the event was described in precise terms. The Prosecutor quite intentionally kept that information back from us; and, quite obviously, we're dealing with a very dangerous criminal. I'll come to why he was released from prison in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in your country and in the proceedings in your country, they are probably not very different from what happens in civil law countries. First of all, the prosecutor draws up an indictment. Before that, the investigating magistrate has conducted an investigation, questioned the suspect with his counsel being present, and so on and so forth. Later on, an indictment is raised against the accused, and the matter is referred to a court on the basis of material, because, otherwise, anybody could be prosecuted before any court without any type of evidence. So I suppose that, if you were prosecuted, there must have been some material at the basis of all this. I would like to know if you were interviewed by an investigative magistrate. I suppose you told him that you had nothing to do with all of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. That's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And despite all of this, the prosecutor decided to have you tried for these crimes; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Against us 136. The legal proceedings were taken against us and a separate group of five of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Yes, Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: One short observation. The accused is insinuating that the Prosecution on purpose did not disclose this sentence or this decision from the Court. I'm sure that we don't have it in our possession because before a witness is coming, we're looking through all our documents, and the documents relevant we disclose to the accused. We cannot disclose something which is not in our possession.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we're not talking about a judgement. If the law on amnesty is in force there is no judgement. It is a decision to apply the law on amnesty that is passed and this frees the accused of any further accountability. So these are two different things, two different legal acts. We need the entire documents, the criminal file, the criminal report, the judgement, the hearing, and the proceedings at trial. We need all this for this witness, and that is something we did not receive. The Prosecution knew about it. If it does not have these documents in its possession, it made no effort to come by them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, might I be allowed to say something, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, legal proceedings were taken against me, and I sat in a court like this for 24 days before 86 witnesses. There is a judgement; Mr. Seselj is not right on that score. Perhaps he is interpreting another piece of law. But in Croatia, in Bjelovar, I was acquitted. A judgement of acquittal was passed because there was not enough evidence. And because of the armed uprising that I took part in, the law on amnesty was applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Seselj, the witness has given us an additional piece of information. According to him, he was acquitted for these crimes and the law on amnesty applied to the armed uprising. That's what the witness is telling us, but you may have the judgement in your possession.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, well, from a hostile state like Croatia, it is the Prosecution that should supply me with the documents, I assume, because neither me nor my associates can travel over there. We can't go there because it's an enemy state, as far as we're concerned, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, nobody's asking you to, and you probably would not have been able to go to Croatia, but nothing prevents you from sending a letter to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They wouldn't have given it to me had I asked for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't need any authorisation from the Chamber to write a letter to Croatia to ask for disclosure of a judgement related to this witness, this Prosecution witness. I am convinced that Croatia would have handed over this document to you. The Prosecution could also have done so, but they decided not to do it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is like a fairytale for me to ask for something for the Croatian authorities and for them to respond and give me what I asked for. That's a fairytale, but it doesn't matter. You, the members of the Trial Chamber, are eye-witnesses to the fact that this witness, during the examination-in-chief, stated here that he was tried in Croatia for the crime in Vocin which took place at a time when he happened to be in Belgrade, and that he was acquitted because he was not on the crime scene. I'm putting a new fact before you now, and the witness has confirmed that he was actually tried for this. Now, for the first time, he's saying that he was acquitted for lack of evidence. I don't know whether we can believe him or not. But if it's truly that way, that he was acquitted because there was not enough evidence, that doesn't mean he did not commit the crime. It only means that the court did not manage to prove it on that occasion. Some other court may be able to prove it sometime. That's the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you were acquitted for lack of evidence; is that what you've said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the indictment against me, Your Honours, not in a single segment of that indictment, or at least that's what my lawyer told me, what my counsel said, was there any element indicating a specific criminal offence. It was a blanket indictment. There was not a specific crime I was accused of. I was only charged with armed rebellion which I did not deny, or rather, I did not deny that I was a member of the Territorial Defence in the manner I have described. Mr. Seselj's constructions have already been seen in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm amazed that you permit the witness to make such comments, what has already been seen on my part in this courtroom. There's really no point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this is the first time you've testified before us. The accused alleges that there was an indictment against you. You agree. You tell us that you were acquitted because there was not enough evidence against you. All very well, and I'm glad for you. That's all. That's the only conclusion we can draw from all of this. Mr. Seselj, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, the strategy of your defence before the court in Croatia was to pass on the responsibility to other people. So with the help of your counsel you tried to blame the chief of the police station in Vocin, Mile Crnobrnja, and Boro Lukic, who was already dead because he was killed later in the war in Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what's correct then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boro Lukic was not killed. He was not dead at the time. I never tried to pass on responsibility onto him or Mile or anybody else. I simply stated, before the court, the facts I had seen and what I had experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What did you say in the court about Mile Crnobrnja, in the Croatian court?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really don't see why I should answer questions as to what I said in my testimony and how you defended myself in the court in 1995 in Bjelovar in connection with these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for a response, Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Vocin is a locality mentioned in the indictment. Crimes were allegedly committed in that locality or around that locality. The accused is charged for crimes committed in this locality by volunteers who were affiliated to the SRS, and at that time the accused was the president of that party. So, apparently, crimes were committed in Vocin. The accused seems to be implying that he has nothing to do with these crimes and even less to do with these volunteers. He's saying that these crimes may have been committed by local people. We find out that there was a trial regarding 20 Croats who allegedly were killed, and it appears that you were prosecuted. You were amongst those prosecuted for these crimes, and that's it. The accused is trying to establish that a number of events took place in Vocin that might be related to other people than the volunteers, but that might be connected to local people and you are one of these locals. That's why he's asking these questions to you. But I'd like to stress that the accused probably has some information. He says that during the trial you, Witness, blamed two persons and he gave us their names. I conclude that the accused probably has some information, maybe because he conducted an investigation or maybe because his associates, his lawyers, gleaned information in the press, in press reports, et cetera. So he's trying to find out who might be responsible for these crimes he's charged with. According to the Prosecution, crimes were committed in Vocin by volunteers of the SRS, and the accused is now trying to establish that others may have committed these crimes. So, please, answer the questions put to you by the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I accept what you said without doubt, but Mr. Seselj did not ask me about the role of particular persons. He asked me what I -- what my testimony was in Bjelovar in 1995. Thirteen years have elapsed since then. How can I remember what I said in my testimony then?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, the witness remembers what happened 17 years ago, and he can't remember what happened 13 years ago. His testimony in the trial against me is not just second-hand but third-hand and forty-third-hand evidence, and yet he directly testified about Mile Crnobrnja and his role. Mile Crnobrnja was the chief of the police station in Vocin. So please make the witness tell us what he said in his testimony concerning Mile Crnobrnja in the court in Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you appeared before that court. You must remember what happened when you blamed other people, especially since it was about establishing that you were innocent and you were acquitted. So do you remember? So please try to answer the questions. Mr. Seselj, please put your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Kulic, is in the court in Bjelovar, what did you state about the role of Mile Crnobrnja in the slaughter of Croatian civilians in Cetekovci, or rather, about the hamlets of Balinci and Cojluk? What did you say there about the role of Mile Crnobrnja, and what entered the record?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what entered the record of those proceedings, Your Honours, but all I could have said was that Mile Crnobrnja, as the commander of the police station in Vocin, the chief of the police station with part of his men participated in the action, and I heard this from other people and men of that unit. There was nothing else I could have said in that connection. If I said anything, I doubt I could have said anything because I didn't know, because I wasn't there at the time. So I knew the people, I knew the structure; that's what I could have said. I could have assumed who was responsible for such an action.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You knew very well who was involved in the slaughter of those Croatian civilians.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know and I don't know now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what did you say about the role of Boro Lukic in that slaughter, in that massacre?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Boro Lukic, I could have only said what I said about Mile Crnobrnja, that he was the most responsible person in the staff at the time. If anyone new about the action, if any planned it, then it would have him, and he would have been responsible on that basis. But that was certainly for the court to establish, and not me, and some other people who were with him in the staff and whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In that staff, you were the senior person by rank, captain first class. Was there any other captain first class there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was a major and another captain first class in that staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who was the major?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The late Boro Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Boro Lukic. Was there any other major?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe someone I didn't know, but I don't know of anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who else was captain first class?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What do you mean by "quite a few of them"?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, five or six, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Give us their names.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, Rajko Bojicic, Keleuva, Jorgic. I can't remember them all but I'm sure that there were more than five.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were they all captains first class or just captains?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were captains first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've promoted them in the meantime, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were people like me from the reserves and they had that rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what happened to Boro Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Boro Lukic, to the best of my knowledge, and I learned this from his family, has died.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where did he die?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He died in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he died -- I can't be precise, but I'll try to remember. I think he died at the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So before your arrest and trial in Bjelovar, right? Boro Lukic died, Mile Crnobrnja fled to Serbia, so you could easily pass the responsibility on to them.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an insinuation and it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, at the time this crime happened, in the immediate vicinity of Vocin, was there any volunteer from Serbia in Western Slavonia? Was there a single volunteer there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So without volunteers from Serbia, some of you in Western Slavonia - not everybody, of course - demonstrated that there were dangerous criminals and cut-throats among you, and that you didn't need volunteers from Serbia to do that because you knew how to cut throats yourself. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how come these Croats were killed, then, if that's not so?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in certain circumstances, Your Honours, and there is evidently no interest or need to explain them here because Mr. Seselj isn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm interested in that very much, and you'll have to answer that question. In what circumstances were these Croatian civilians killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a number of civilian Croats were killed. That's not the matter that's been referred to us. On the other hand, we have been seized about what took place in Vocin regarding what volunteers from the SRS may have done. Apparently, a crime was committed, and you say that there weren't any SRS volunteers there. Those who committed this crime in this locality were local people. They were not volunteers from the SRS coming from Serbia. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there was not a single volunteer from Serbia, not just a volunteer from the Serbian Radical Party. There were no volunteers from Serbia at all, only local people. That's the gist of it, if you let me continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kulic, evidently this mass crime - and there is no doubt it was committed - can in no way be linked to volunteers from Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And all these people who perpetrated that crime in Cetekovci or in the hamlets of Cetekovci so that you don't correct me, they all continued living and working in Western Slavonia within the Territorial Defence. They were all part of the Territorial Defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All the people from Vocin who committed a crime against more than 20 Croatian civilians in Cetekovci in September 1991, after the crime, continued living in Vocin and the surrounding area as if nothing had happened; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must say here that it's not quite correct for the following reason: This was the time when I came to Vocin, and I know that no one talked about that event, at least not in front of me, so that I learned information about that crime only subsequently, a year later even, more from the press than from other people. People didn't talk about it. The answer to the question you put is, yes, most probably those people continued living there because I don't know by name who the perpetrators were and who participated. If I knew, I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So, evidently, there was more than one perpetrator because there was an attack on the village of Cetekovci and 20 Croatian civilians were killed in different ways; some from firearms, some with knives, some with other objects, in various ways. One can see that from the photographs shown to you by the Croatian authorities. All these criminals who remained unpunished could perpetrate more crimes, they could perpetrate more crimes without punishment; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then in the second half of October, volunteers turn up from Serbia and it's very convenient to pass every subsequent crime that happened on to these volunteers and blame them.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I never heard anyone blame volunteers from Serbia for the crime we have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, not this crime but for other future crimes, other crimes that happened, because it's justifiable to assume that these people who committed a mass crime on one occasion were ready and willing to commit crimes elsewhere. They did so in October, November, and December. They found it most convenient as of the second half of October to blame nameless volunteers from Serbia for all subsequent crimes, and that was the standard practice of that group of criminals from Western Slavonia. Isn't that correct, Mr. Kulic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what is correct, then? Those who committed the crime in Cetekovci never committed any other crimes? They repented? They showed remorse? They became good, humane people, and committed no further crimes? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what's not correct? Did they commit more crimes or didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one blamed or accused anyone without grounds, especially not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Crimes were committed in September by members of the TO. We agree on that. Everybody agrees on that. Later on, in October, November, in the following weeks, other crimes were committed. Someone could think that those who committed the first crimes may have committed the others. But in order not to face any responsibility for their crimes, they blame the crimes that took place in October, November, December, they blame these crimes on those volunteers coming from Serbia who may not be very disciplined; and, in doing so, they avoid any type of responsibility. This is just an assumption, an hypothesis. I'm not saying it's the truth but it's something we should take into account. What do you have to say about this? That's the question put to you by Mr. Seselj. What do you have to say about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat, Your Honour. As to the events in Cetekovci, I learnt about them subsequently, much later; and there's absolutely no question Mr. Seselj has no evidence or proof. He's just trying to blacken me in order to further his defence case in the trial. Now, I wish him every success but not by throwing mud on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, we base this on the assumption that you've got nothing to do with it, because you say that you were not there when the crimes were committed. But we're faced with the following situation: There are members of the Territorial Defence who were involved in the commission of crimes and these same people are still part of the Territorial Defence. You don't know this, but these individuals are part of the Territorial Defence. You don't know that in September they have already committed crimes. What would prevent them from continuing and from setting light to houses and killing the Matanci family, for instance? What would prevent them from doing that, and then to lay the blame on the Serb volunteers? We don't know where they come from. All we know is that they come from Serbia and that they belong to the Serbian Radical Party. So is this something which one could imagine, or would it be totally out of bounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible. It's a logical assumption. But what I'm telling you is what happened over there, not what the possibilities are, what is possible and what is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But everything you are saying as having happened over there, it's secondhand. You weren't an eye-witness yourself. Somebody somewhere told you about the fact that the volunteers had carried out this crime and that crime and so forth, but none of those crimes were crimes that you saw with your very own eyes. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see them with my own eyes, any of the crimes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So all your knowledge as to the alleged crimes committed by the volunteers are second-hand knowledge or third-hand, fifth-hand. It's the story that was going around, the rumours being told.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is correct, then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned, Your Honours, that I was there at the time and that I still live there today. I live there again now. So I meet people who were confronted with these crimes, directly confronted, and I have no reason not to believe these people. They did not speak to me within the frameworks of a trial or under pressure or anything like that. They told me about these events because they needed to say what had happened. They needed to recount it. They sympathise with the victims or they were frightened at a certain point in time and weren't able to talk about it earlier on, but now they're free to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How come, Mr. Kulic, that they are ready to talk to you about all the crimes except the first mass crime, the one from Cetekovci? They're perfectly prepared to give you their views and tell you everything they know about the other crimes; whereas, nobody has said a word about this particular crime. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, those people -- it's not that those people couldn't wait to unburden themselves to me. It is that working to help these people return to their homes and living with them today, in many cases and in many instances, we were -- I was in a position to evoke the various stories. There were a lot of people who were tried against whom criminal reports were made, so repeated things of this kind. I didn't know many of the things they told me, but it's not difficult to draw a conclusion and an assumption. If you know the facts and circumstances well and the participants, then you can draw your own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you testified on the basis of your assumptions; isn't that right, Mr. Kulic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't understand the question. It's such a wide question that I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kulic, after the crime in Cetekovci, you commanded the reconnaissance unit of the Territorial Defence in Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, who did command the reconnaissance detachment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was no reconnaissance detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You formed a reconnaissance detachment yourself.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the request of the command, I certainly did take part in the training and organisation of individual sections or individuals and groups in reconnoitring and reconnaissance work, scouting, but I didn't organise that. That wasn't my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You patrolled along the Slatinic-Galina-Lipovac road, didn't you, Mr. Kulic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was never in a patrol. I never patrolled an area, but I did tour certain areas and the names of the villages mentioned are not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, maybe the names of the villages are not correct, I can't see them well to read them; but, on one occasion, you set up an ambush and killed Zvonko Cubeljic and wounded a certain Sikic who was a Croat, and they were unarmed. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one minute. Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Seselj, and we will have to have a short break before resuming again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We came to the point where you killed and ambushed Zvonko Cubeljic and wounded Sikic. They were Croats, unarmed. Isn't that right, Mr. Kulic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not right, Mr. Seselj. Your Honours, I never took part in an armed action anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who killed Zvonko Cubeljic, then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who does? Do you know that Zvonko Cubeljic was killed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Zvonko Cubeljic was killed, Your Honours, because he worked as a caretaker in the building is that I worked in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's why you killed him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an insinuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, you killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This person, Zvonko Cubeljic, according to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I heard from members of his family that he had been killed. That is true, that he was killed. But that has nothing to do with me, and the insinuation made by Mr. Seselj that I killed anybody anywhere is following the same logic that he's been following up to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, in an ambush you, did kill a Croat and the surname of that man was Minauf. He was in a kombi van. He was a civilian driving in a van. You organised an ambush and killed him. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who killed him, then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who killed him. I do know that he was killed, but let me repeat, Your Honours, I never took part in the area of Vocin in any armed action in which there were wounded or killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was Minauf's name?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you do know about the killing?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I urge you not to put criminal incriminations to a witness without your being able to prove it. If you can prove it, let's see it; otherwise, stay away from incriminating a witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, I am presenting the facts that are general knowledge to everyone from Western Slavonia, and I am going to provide you with many statements, authenticated in court, which confirm that by people who know, and we'll start with those statements in a few minutes' time. Perhaps, after the break, we'll be looking at some of those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The best will be to have the break now. We shall have a 10-minute break because we have a limited amount of time. We shall have a 10-minute break and resume in 10 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing. Now, as far as our timing is concerned, Mr. Seselj, you've had 28 minutes so far. So you have one hour and 32 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [No interpretation] In paragraph 32 -- May I begin? In the statement that you gave in 2007, let me see, on the 14th of November, 2007, to be exact, in paragraph 32, you stated that in December 1991, when you were in the office of Western Slavonia in Belgrade, you met a man who introduced himself as being somebody who was sending volunteers to Western Slavonia on behalf of the Radical Party. Is that really what you said?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's what it says in the paragraph, then I probably said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it wasn't at the headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party and its war staff but in the offices of Western Slavonia in Belgrade, the Western Slavonian office in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's how it was, just the way you put it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you weren't in the offices of the Serbian Radical Party at all, were you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there on one occasion in Ohridska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where is that street?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's above Zeleni Venac, the marketplace. What's it called? When you go down Balkanska Street, well, I'm not very familiar with Belgrade, but you can go to Ohridska Street if you take that Balkanska Street. There's a number of non-governmental offices there, so I know where the area is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: From Balkanska Street, Mr. Kulic, you emerge on top of Zeleni Venac market.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But it's a long way off from Ohridska Street, and there's no non-governmental organisation in the building where the Serbian Radical Party had its headquarters, not a single one. Ohridska Street was near the Svetosavska church. Do you know how far that is from Balkanska Street?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A long way off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you don't know where the Serbian Radical Party has its headquarters at all?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know because I went past that way. It's visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The present headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the 1991 headquarters, where the head offices were then.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how do you say that you were in the seat of the Serbian Radical Party if you don't know where it is?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I repeat: I was going there with a man who was on his way there. I just happened to be there by chance because I met this person that I knew from before and I went with him. So I didn't claim that I knew where the headquarters were or the headquarters of the war staff, and I was taken there by that man. I am convinced that I was in the war staff office because I had met Mr. Petkovic whom I met before once.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What does Ljubisa Petkovic look like?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he looked like, Your Honours? Well, I could perhaps describe that. What he looks like now, that would be more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. What did he look like then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was a rather tall person of a pleasant disposition, brown hair. He's taller than me. I don't know how to describe him. No specific characteristic features.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You say he's taller than you. How much taller?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You say brown hair.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has a photograph of Mr. Ljubisa Petkovic. But how tall are you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 173 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Ljubisa Petkovic is at least a head shorter than you. He is very short, very thin, has dark black hair and a black moustache.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honours, it seems I mixed these people up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you never talked to Ljubisa Petkovic because you don't even know what he looks like. Now we're going to see what Ljubisa Petkovic says about all this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be placed on the overhead projector because it arrived by fax yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj and Mr. Kulic, please do not forget to observe a small pause between your questions and answers because it puts the interpreters in great difficulty because they can't follow you, simply.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you got that in front of you, Mr. Kulic, on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have it before me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I haven't got it on my screen yet. I have it now. Now, would you read out this statement by Ljubisa Petkovic. You don't have to read the top part, but where it says "I hereby declare or state ..." and then after that. Read it out loud, please, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I state that I don't know a single person named Mladen Kulic, absolutely nobody with that first and last name. When the name Mladen Kulic is mentioned or I hear the name, the first and last name, I have no recollections of that, nor does it give rise to any associations with respect to an individual or any territory. That first and last name means absolutely nothing to me."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The person who says his name is Mladen Kulic, I never talked to that person, nor did I ever see that person with my own eyes. If somebody introduces himself or deemed Mladen Kulic and says that he talked to me, Ljubisa Petkovic, then all he is saying is a blatant lie. "If somebody named Mladen Kulic claims that he held a meeting with me, Ljubisa Petkovic, in Belgrade or any other place, then he is stating a lie, because quite simply I, Ljubisa Petkovic, never had a meeting with a person named Mladen Kulic, nor did I talk to him. "I'm giving this statement of my own free will and I'm fully conscious of my responsibilities, and I allow Professor Dr. Vojislav Seselj to use this before the MKSJ and any other proceedings and organs. As I am a witness of the Defence, Mr. Vojislav Seselj considers that I'm best placed to tell the truth."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You see that this was given in the Belgrade court. So do you still claim that you ever met Ljubisa Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do claim, Your Honours, that I met Ljubisa Petkovic, if it is the same person who signed the document on sending the first group of volunteers to Ceralije.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But, you see, you've described him quite wrongly. You say that he was taller than you and had brown hair. The Prosecution knows that Ljubisa Petkovic is much shorter than you. He is perhaps 20 -- well, he is so thin he might be 20 kilogrammes. He is exceptionally dark and has a dark moustache. The Prosecution knows that full well. They have a photograph of him; and by pressing the button, they can show you that photograph. So you can't describe him. You don't know where Ohridska Street was, which was the headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party. You've located it wrongly near Balkanska Street and Zeleni Venac market. Ljubisa Petkovic, himself, claims that he's never heard you, never in his life, and that he never met you either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a serious problem. In the course of the afternoon, I asked you to describe Mr. Petkovic's office, which you did. Now either you're lying, or Mr. Petkovic is lying with this statement, or, third alternative, you went to the headquarters of the SRS and somebody went there pretending to be Petkovic. How do things stand, as far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, everything I said is true. The truth dates from 1991 or early 1992. That truth is burdened with the passage of 17 years. I won't try to persuade anyone in something I'm not sure of. But with respect to the headquarters of the Radical Party, or rather, the war staff - that's what they called it - I didn't equate it with a party headquarters; that's one thing. And, secondly, as for my familiarity with Belgrade, well, I'm really very poor in that. If you were to ask me where the bureau of Western Slavonia is, where I visited more than once - I knew the people - it's a moot point whether I would be able to explain it clearly after all this time, even though I was there. So it's quite clear that when it comes to familiarity with Belgrade and this office, I may be wrong, but I was there only in passing, simply in passing. Mr. Petkovic was introduced to me by people from the bureau. And with respect to this case of the volunteers, I spoke about it to a person who introduced himself to me as such. I can't say that I know some people from my immediate environment as well. And if this is a faithful description, as Mr. Seselj says, then evidently I may have mistook the person, but it was not my intention to invent anything or to tell lies. Quite simply, I cannot with precision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 40 of your written statement, you say that you went to see Petkovic because you were concerned about the security of the local population. You mentioned that four young Croatians had disappeared, and so on and so forth, and that these incidents were connected to the volunteers who were out of control, violent, and committed crimes at the time. Is this what the investigator wants you to say or is this what you told the investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There is no doubt that I said this to the investigator of the Prosecution. But when you mention these events, they differ in time. My information about the circumstances regarding these four lads came from after the events in Western Slavonia. When it comes to the encounter with Mr. Petkovic in the bureau of Western Slavonia, this happened immediately after the exodus; and, quite simply, it was a conversation in which I did not look for Mr. Petkovic. He was there with those people, but I'm not claiming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many times did you see Mr. Petkovic, once or twice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the office of Western Slavonia, I met him. He was introduced to me as that person. And later on, with Captain Zarko and someone else, I went there once again. I think I was in the war staff, that is, but it was certainly not the same place. I know that the bureau was in the former general staff, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You saw him twice, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you saw him at the war staff office, that's when you told him about these four young men who had been killed, or was it at the office of Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the bureau of Western Slavonia, I only pointed out that when I left I said to him and to the three or four people who were there, Mr. Simpraga and this other gentleman who I always thought up to now was Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you went to the war staff in Belgrade, what did you want to talk to him about when you went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not go there intentionally or look for him. I went with Mr. Zarko Loncarevic. He was an officer, and I went with him in passing. It was not my intention to go. But I encountered the person and I thought up to this point that he was Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Be careful because you have professional Judges sitting before you, professional Judges with years of experience. Now I'm going to confront you with your contradictions. You state that you met Mr. Petkovic on two occasions. Apparently, when you went to see him in Belgrade at the war staff, you met with someone and you were supposed to meet that person again at the bureau for Western Slavonia. It had to be the same person. But the description you give of this individual does not seem to correspond to what Petkovic looks like. Does it mean that you met on two occasions a Petkovic who was not the right Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have mistaken the person, but up till now I was convinced that was the person. I link that person with the document on which I had occasion to see the name of the person. That's why I link it up and for no other reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the bureau for Western Slavonia, when exactly, at what time, did you meet Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in mid-December 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mid-December 1991. When you saw Mr. Petkovic at the Main Staff in Belgrade, when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the staff in Belgrade, I'm convinced I saw him in the course of February 1992, and that's what I said in my testimony. I think it was February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. February 1992. Two months later, did you meet this same and exact person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes. It was the same person, but I cannot assert now that that person had that name because it's been brought into doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, so now you have a doubt. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the way of comparison, the shape and the link-up with the name, it's evident that the person I met was not a person called Petkovic. But I thought I had met Petkovic; I was convinced I had met Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the one you saw in December and February is the same person. Let's assume we meet again in two months' time; and if suddenly you have dark hair and you are two metres tall, then I could not mix you up with that person. But you tell me that the person you met in December and the person you met in February was the same person; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if the one you met in December and February is not Petkovic, because apparently it does not correspond to him, apparently somebody passed himself off as Petkovic on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I allow that someone introduced the person to me, not that the person introduced himself to me, because the forms of introduction are not so strict among people who are acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: As court participants, we are in a position to show a photograph of Ljubisa Petkovic if it's allowed. Should we do this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please show it. We'll see what he looks like, then. Witness, is this the man you saw in December and February?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's hard to assert this because there were very many people there and also a lot of time has elapsed. Really, there are lots of people who look a bit like this, who have similar faces. So I do not want to make a mistake again. I can neither say that I saw him, nor that I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we keep the picture on the screen for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you see that this person has brown hair, Mr. Kulic? Is it evident that he has brown hair?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That his hair is brown?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the picture, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what colour hair is it, then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's dark. It may be black.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can it be darker than this? Do you see that he is a man of slight build? And this man here whose shoulder you can just glimpse, do you see how much bigger he is? Why are you quiet, Mr. Kulic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, in December when I was in Belgrade, although you're a big man, Dr. Seselj, even if he were bigger than you, I wouldn't remember, because the circumstances I was in personally and everybody else, I may have made a mistake here. But if the person in the picture I see was working on those issues, then I'm sure I met him, too. But I can't explain this, Your Honour. It's a question of whether I could describe anyone I had seen in that period of time precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kulic, that's precisely what I am trying to show, that you are unable to describe anything from that period of time. In paragraph 40 you, said that in mid-December 1991, while you were in Belgrade, you went to see Petkovic because you were concerned over the safety of the local population; so not in February, in December. It's in paragraph 40.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question of December, well, that's either when the exodus had already taken place or was about to take place. But in any case at that time, at a later date than the exodus, I can't know with precision whether it had taken place or not because communication was poor, but I know that I was in the government bureau around -- because of that issue to see how to protect those people and concerning the general situation. In the bureau, they told me that the person who was there-- it wasn't someone who had been sought, but someone in the bureau said there's a person here whom you can tell this to. In February I was -- I went to Belgrade with a senior officer on official business, and he took me there. I didn't go looking for the war staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were given a photograph of Ljubisa Petkovic by the OTP. Did you see that person in the government bureau of Western Slavonia, in the headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party, whether you visited that headquarters in December or February? Did you meet that man as Ljubisa Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, right now I cannot say what I met and what that person looked like whom I met under that name, and I cannot bring into question this picture because my memory, after 17 years, with all the people who have passed through my life in the meantime and everything I've been through, this now makes me wonder whether I can remember with such precision, especially when this man says I never saw him. He can say that but I could not mistake the first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, let's say I believe you, that you arrived in Ohridska Street, in the headquarters of the war staff. Did you see an inscription over the doorway, the entrance to the building? What did it say? There weren't any NGOs there except for that one. What did it say?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when it comes to mentioning Ohridska Street as the premises of the war staff, quite evidently, after mentioning my testimony here, obviously I was mistaken. I was convinced that that was the street called -- well, the one going from Balkanska Street up the green-belt. But I may have become confused because I don't know Belgrade well to pinpoint with precision the headquarters of the party and the premises of the war staff. As has been mentioned here, I passed by there. I know that part about above Slavija but not so well. I don't know the names and addresses. So, Your Honour, I can't recall what Dr. Seselj is asking about; that is, I can't remember the shape of the inscription above the entrance to the building in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Was there a flag flying from that building?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot allow myself now to speculate. I cannot recall with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. But there's one thing you should be able to remember. If you entered the building where the headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party was and its war staff, on what floor was it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, Your Honours, that my colleague Zarko contacted someone who led us into the building, and we were in two rooms, I think, until he found someone he was looking for. And from the ground floor, I think we climbed up the stairs to the first floor, but I can't even be sure about that, on what floor those premises were, because quite simply immediately after that we went to the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, and after that we went to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. So I visited several buildings at that time. So if you were to ask me precisely about a place I visited more than once, for example, the bureau of the Government of Serbia, I think it was on the ground floor, but I wouldn't be surprised to hear that it was on the mezzanine, although I visited it more than once.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's cut this short, Mr. President. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you meet Colonel Jovan Trbojevic in Western Slavonia? He was the commander of the Territorial Defence there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your honours, Could Mr. Seselj be more specific when he said "meet," where, when?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, in any way. Did you see him? Did you meet him anywhere??

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in that way, I did meet Colonel Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I talked to him twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did he ever speak to you about his opinions with respect to the arrival of the Serbian Radical Party to Western Slavonia? Did he ever speak about that to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was not in a position to have Colonel Trbojevic explain to me that, but I did it in two meetings with officers which was presided over by Colonel Trbojevic. So except for the question of subordination, I don't remember that he mentioned any other issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did any of the officers ever complain about the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The company commander from Ceralije, he complained. And I was with a group of people in the staff at Vocin, and there was a threat from a group of Radical Party volunteers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you now place this statement by Colonel Jovan Trbojevic on the overhead, please. It was certified in the Municipal Court in Belgrade. It is a three-page document but we're just going to look at three short paragraphs and read them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the first time we see these documents. It would be very useful to get these documents in advance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It reached me by fax today, and you can see the date when it was faxed on the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not really a problem because the Judges are seeing this document for the first time; and as true professionals, we'll be able to review the document immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it can be copied. I'll leave it for you to see. But I'm interested in three key sentences in this document, and the Prosecution will be provided with the document in its entirety. I haven't got it on my screen yet. Have you got it on yours? Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kulic, on page 1, I have marked an excerpt with my pen, so read that portion out, just the organisation underlined.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "About the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, Radovan Novacic and Vojislav Seselj, I can state with full responsibility on this occasion that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party remain in my memory as disciplined fighters, that they acted exclusively under the command of the TO, and that throughout their time on the battlefield of Western Slavonia, they displayed exceptional bravery and helped the Serbian population in the area that were under threat. I can thank the Radicals for responding to the request of the TO from that area and for the fact that they came to my native region."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now turn to the next page, and this excerpt here pencilled in, read that out, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "When I arrived in Western Slavonia, that was during the time of the arrival of the volunteers. Some 500 of them arrived. Of that number, 250 remained in Okucani. They were sent to units which were subordinated to the corps and the other half was sent to me under my command; that is to say, the territory of Papuk. "A busload was in the region of Daruvar and another group was in the region of the staff of TO Slatina. Volunteers arrived in groups, and I know that they did not belong to Vojislav Seselj and the Serbian Radical Party. Based on my knowledge, they were volunteers who belonged to Niko Jovic and Vuk Draskovic, and their commander was a retired officer whom they did not respect and it was an impediment. "This was a problematic group and they were put up in Vocin. To the best of my knowledge, they took part in the torching of houses of Matanci family. Those who were under the supervision of Radovan Novacic were accommodated in Lager Sekulinci, 11 kilometres from Vocin, and in the village of Koricani, which is some 30 kilometres from Vocin in Daruvar municipality. "That Novacic group deserved every praise, and I told that to the Hague Tribunal which they held against me. I said that Radovan Novacic was excellent and that he always had permission from me when he told the volunteers to do anything."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And another sentence on the next page, the one pencilled in again.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party left Vocin five days before the liquidation of 32 persons, 29 Croats and 3 Serbs. The liquidation took place on the 13th of December, 1991, and the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party left that territory on the 8th of December, 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kulic.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, Colonel Jovan Trbojevic is going to be a Defence witness at this trial, so you'll have an opportunity to question him in depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kulic, what do you think about these excerpts from Colonel Jovan Trbojevic's statement? Is he telling the truth or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's difficult to assume that a commander of the staff of Western Slavonia does not know what paramilitary formations he has, but I'm quite sure that Colonel Trbojevic, because of his honour, well, I would say that he spoke the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kulic. Now, several times, in your statement, you said that you're not able to differentiate between the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party from the White Eagles, Draskovic's volunteers, and so on and so forth, and that you're not able to distinguish from these groups. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So, as far as you're concerned, all the volunteers looked the same and you considered them to be a compact mass. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was convinced, Your Honours, that the volunteers were one formation which came under one form of command and that they were people from the same group affiliated to the same entity. I was convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that between the political parties that sent the volunteers to the territory, the Serbian Radical Party, the Serbian Renewal Movement, and so on, and that there was political hostility throughout, between all these parties?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I do know that certain differences existed. But I don't know anything more specific on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, we're now going to go back to part of your statement which relates to the formation of the Serbian Democratic Party. We don't have much time but we can get through that segment. Now, during the examination-in-chief, you stressed the difficult position that the Serbian people found themselves in, in Croatia, after Tudjman's victory in the elections, and you also said what those first parliamentary elections looked like and who the Serbs voted for. You came to the formation of the Serbian Democratic Party. Then, in your statement, you said, and that is the statement of 9th of October, and to the 11th of May, 2002, on page 3 of that statement, you said that you did not attend the convention of the Serbian Democratic Party in the autumn of 1990 in Podravska Slatina because you didn't like the people who were there and their ideas. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of the party because of that -- those kinds of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you said here that the first reason why you didn't like their ideas was the fact that it was their national idea which was negligible compared to the idea that you supported up until then, the concept of brotherhood and unity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then you said you didn't like their nationalistic spirit, nor the fact that they caused incidents, nor the fact that they were able to manipulate people easily. In other words, they grouped themselves in some sort of gang or band. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never used the word "gang" or "band," least of all for my own people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's place document 0306-5128 on the ELMO now, please, or have it up on e-court. Do you have the document? I have the number and the Prosecutor provided me with the number. It is a document dated 1992. And if you remember, Judges, it was the document I asked the Prosecution to provide me for and they didn't want to do that on time. So let's put this on the overhead projector, paragraph 3 from the bottom. Whenever I look for something and ask for something, I always have good reason for doing that. I hope I have shown you that, and the Prosecution always have a reason for not providing me with a particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Read that paragraph out. It's your statement. You signed it. Would you read it outloud, please?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The main reason why I didn't like their ideas is that their national idea was trivial compared to the idea or ideal that I had supported until then, which was the idea of brotherhood and unity which was much broader and indicated multi-culturalism and unity between people of different nationality. I didn't like their nationalistic spirit either, nor the fact that they caused incidents, nor people who were easily manipulated. In other words, they associated themselves into some sort of gang or band." I distanced myself from this. Even if I signed that, I would never sign that now. Now, how this was translated or where this formulation comes from, I don't know. I certainly wouldn't have described it in that way because that wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you signed the statement in 1992, did you sign it in English or in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't remember. I cannot remember the text. I think there was both the English version and the Serbian version, or perhaps just the English version. But I can't be sure now. I can't say for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But this doesn't correspond to what you told the investigators before they wrote your statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This text and this particular description certainly is not the right one. I would never use that word. I would never say it that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Judges, why I don't allow any statement to be introduced under 92 ter because I come across this same situation with every witness. Every witness denies having said certain things, and I think that was useful to be pointed out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, in several places --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we'll stop for now because it's just about time. We'll stop with this witness, and I need to talk about tomorrow's witness. So you will be coming back tomorrow for the rest of the cross-examination. The hearing will start at a quarter to 3.00 tomorrow, and you will finish tomorrow, because I believe, Mr. Seselj, you have approximately one hour left. I don't have the exact countdown. Madam Usher, could you escort the witness out of the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have had 57 minutes. You will have one hour and three minutes left. There was only a three-minute differential. So just, in a few minutes, to say that tomorrow we plan to hear a witness whose name I will not give because he will benefit from voice distortion and face distortion. His pseudonym will be 21. This is a 92 ter procedure, 92 ter witness, so we have a written statement which everybody has. This has been authenticated by the witness. The written statement contains 67 paragraphs. The Prosecution intends to adduce a number of documents, not very many of them. We have some photographs and two documents. There will be five documents all in all. So the Prosecution will have 30 minutes. That will be ample to give us a brief summary of the written statement, put questions to the witness, and show the exhibits to the witness. After that, the Defence of Mr. Seselj will have an hour and a half to cross-examine the witness. If, Mr. Seselj, you do not wish to cross-examine this witness, you are perfectly entitled to do so. You cannot cross-examine him if you so wish. But you must let us know. Maybe you will tell us that you do not wish to cross-examine him. If you do not wish to cross-examine him at all, the Bench can then put a few questions to the witness based on the written statement which pertains for the main part to what happened in the hospital of Vukovar before, during, and after. So this for the main part will relate to the Vukovar Hospital. So once we have finished with this witness, we will have a 92 ter procedure. If you wish to put your questions, you may; if you don't wish to put your questions, you won't. This is what I wanted to tell you, Mr. Seselj. You can think about it until tomorrow. So far you have demonstrated your ability at putting relevant and interesting questions, so I don't see why you should not put any questions during the cross-examination or based on the written statement which is very simple; and, to my mind, this is not an issue at all. Your cross-examination could highlight a number of facts. If you don't wish to do it, so be it. But the Bench believes - I am speaking on behalf of all the Judges of this Bench - the Witness VS-21, well, what is interested as far as we're concerned is what happened in Vukovar, who committed the crimes, and who these crimes can be blamed on, if there is any connection with the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. So this is why this witness may be an interesting witness for all of us. Now, if you would like to say something, please do so now because we need to finish very soon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly. First, never in my life am I going to question a witness under 92 ter, 92 bis, or 92 quater. You might bring someone in under that rule. So there's no reason to discuss that further. But another point is this: I want you to explain to me the following: How is it possible that this particular witness, Mladen Kulic, is testifying viva voce about the crime base in Western Slavonia; whereas, you made rulings several times that evidence, crime base evidence, in Western Slavonia is not going to be presented? Now, everything that this witness testified about was second-hand testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has been taken off the indictment, but the deliberate conduct has remained, and this was to establish that what happened in Vocin illustrates what happened in other areas. So this decision was handed down not by this Chamber but by a previous Chamber. So what we're interested in is a deliberate line of conduct and this pattern of conduct is what we want to establish. This is why this witness came to testify in this case; to establish that volunteers may have committed some crimes. You have highlighted a number of facts during your cross-examination and these facts are relevant and interesting. If you do not cross-examine the witness, you will not be able to highlight a number of things. Vukovar is not part of the pattern of conduct; and as far as Vukovar is concerned, we need to understand when hearing Prosecution witnesses and Defence witnesses and hearing what you have to say, because you have said that you wish to testify, we want to understand what actually happened in Vukovar because the Trial Chamber needs to draw its conclusion. I'm a little bit surprised by the fact that you are depriving yourself of the possibility of cross-examining the witness which could highlight a number of things which would be in favour of your defence, to rebut the Prosecution's position. This is your own personal choice, but I would like to tell you that this could be risky for you. The Prosecution will put questions tomorrow, the Bench will put questions tomorrow; and, perhaps, in the end, you will say that you do not wish to put any questions to the witness. So we shall stop for today and resume tomorrow again at a quarter to three. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 6th day of March, 2008, at 2.45 p.m. 16 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
